claims.text: Research on algorithmic discrimination in credit is predominantly conducted from Computer Science and Economics domain perspectives.
Credit domain discrimination research focuses mostly on direct discrimination, while indirect structural discrimination remains significantly under-studied.
The mortgage approval gap between Black and White applicants in the US decreases from 7% to 3.5% towards the end of the month.
Same-sex loan co-applicants in the US are 73% more likely to be denied or receive higher interest/fee rates compared to different-sex co-applicants.
Non-linear machine learning scoring models magnify existing disparities in credit data compared to traditional linear logit credit scoring models.
FinTech mortgage lenders process loan applications 20% faster than traditional commercial banks.

evidence.description: Meta-analysis of 78 literature review papers showed primary concentration in Computer Science (CS) and Economics (ECO) domains.

Systematic review results state that researchers are still only dealing with direct discrimination, addressed by algorithmic fairness, while indirect discrimination (structural discrimination) has not received the same attention.
Analysis of 25 years of HMDA mortgage data (Yu 2022, Giacoletti et al. 2021) shows approval rates increase towards month-end and the Black-White approval gap drops from 7% to 3.5%.
Empirical evidence from US mortgage data analyzed by Sun and Gao (2019) demonstrated same-sex co-applicants were 73% more likely to be denied or charged higher fees.
Bono et al. (2021) and Fuster et al. (2022) empirically and mathematically showed non-linear ML credit models boost slight data differences, expanding group outcome gaps compared to logit models.
Fuster et al. (2019) evaluated FHA mortgage data from 2010 to 2016, finding FinTech lenders offered 20% faster processing times than traditional banks.

methodologies.name: Systematic Literature Review Protocol
methodologies.description: A systematic literature review following Kitchenham's protocol exploring five digital databases to identify, screen, and synthesize 78 relevant studies on credit domain algorithmic discrimination published between 2017 and 2022.

limitations.text: The identification of first author sex and race/ethnicity relied on visual perception of names and online facial images, representing an approximation rather than self-reported demographic data.
Multiple core group fairness metrics (calibration within groups, balance for negative class, balance for positive class) cannot be satisfied simultaneously except under perfect prediction conditions.
Credit scoring datasets suffer from intrinsic selection bias and missing labels because loan default is only observed for approved applicants.

future_work.text: Develop algorithmic fairness approaches that evaluate and mitigate bias across multiple sensitive attributes simultaneously using intersectionality theory.
Investigate reverse redlining and skin-tone discrimination in Global South and developing countries using large-scale credit datasets.
Establish societal consensus and regulatory frameworks regarding privacy trade-offs when expanding non-traditional data sources for unbanked applicants.
